symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with characteristic concentric rings ('bullseye' pattern) on older leaves.
Yellow halos often surround the circular spots as they expand.
Lower foliage yellows, withers, and eventually drops off prematurely.
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions can form on stems and near the stem-end of fruit.
prevention: Practice a 2- to 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops (tomatoes, potatoes, eggplants).
Ensure proper plant spacing and staking to maximize airflow and sunlight penetration.
Water at the base using drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage; avoid overhead watering.
Apply organic mulch around plants to prevent soil-borne fungal spores from splashing onto foliage.
management: Prune and remove infected lower leaves early in the morning on dry days.
Dispose of infected plant residues; do not compost diseased material.
Maintain balanced soil nutrition; avoid excessive nitrogen that promotes lush, susceptible foliage.
Consult local agricultural extension agents for regional bio-fungicide or copper-based preventive programs.
Tomato___Early_blight.limitations: Early blight symptoms can occasionally mimic Septoria leaf spot or physical leaf scorching in early stages.
references: Penn State Extension - Tomato Early Blight IPM Guide

symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked pale green or dark brown lesions rapidly spreading across leaves.
White fungal-like fuzzy growth on the undersides of leaves during humid or wet weather.
Dark brown to black lesions on petioles and stems.
Firm, rough, olive-brown sunken patches on green or ripening fruit.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free transplants and resistant cultivars when available.
Avoid planting tomatoes adjacent to or following potatoes.
Eliminate cull piles and volunteer tomato and potato plants in the vicinity.
Maintain good canopy ventilation and avoid overhead irrigation.
management: Late blight spreads aggressively; infected plants must be removed immediately to protect neighboring crops.
Bag and remove infected tissues from the field; do not leave discarded vines nearby.
Monitor local late-blight forecasting networks and extension alerts.
Consult certified plant pathologists for region-approved protective fungicide protocols.
Tomato___Late_blight.limitations: Late blight moves extremely fast in cool, wet conditions (60-70°F). Rapid physical inspection is critical.

symptoms: Pale green to yellowish spots with indistinct margins on the upper leaf surface.
Olive-green to brown velvety fungal growth on the corresponding lower surface.
Infected leaves eventually turn yellow, curl, wither, and drop prematurely.
prevention: Common in high tunnels and greenhouses; maximize ventilation to keep relative humidity below 85%.
Space plants generously to promote rapid drying of foliage.
Circulate air with fans and avoid wetting foliage during irrigation.
management: Prune lower foliage to improve vertical airflow within greenhouse canopies.
Sanitize greenhouse structures, stakes, and tools between planting cycles.
Consult agricultural extension services for resistant tomato varieties and authorized treatments.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.limitations: Leaf mold predominantly occurs in humid protected environments; less common in open arid field settings.

symptoms: Small (1/8 inch), water-soaked, dark brown or black angular spots on leaves.
Centers of lesions may dry out and tear, creating a ragged or shot-hole appearance.
Blister-like, scabby, or rough brown spots on green fruit.
Severe infections lead to general leaf yellowing and extensive defoliation.
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water treated seeds and healthy transplants.
Sanitize greenhouse flats, stakes, and pruning shears with standard disinfectant.
Avoid working in or harvesting fields while foliage is wet from rain or dew.
Implement a minimum 2-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops.
management: Remove and destroy severely infected seedlings before field transplanting.
Copper-based bactericides combined with mancozeb may slow spread when applied preventively.
Consult regional agronomy specialists for diagnostic confirmation and local resistance patterns.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.limitations: Bacterial diseases do not respond to fungal fungicides. Distinguishing bacterial spot from speck requires close examination.
references: University of Florida Vegetable Production Handbook

symptoms: Uniform vibrant green leaves with well-defined margins and natural leaf texture.
No visible chlorosis, necrosis, bullseye spots, water-soaking, or fungal sporulation.
Vigorous stem and leaf node development.
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture and balanced macro- and micro-nutrient fertility.
Inspect plants weekly for early signs of pest presence or environmental stress.
Practice crop rotation and sanitize equipment between seasons.
management: Continue routine cultural care and regular pest monitoring.
Support plant stems with clean stakes or trellises as vines mature.
Tomato___healthy.limitations: Healthy appearance at one time does not preclude asymptomatic latent infections or root pathogens.

symptoms: Small, dark brown to black spots with concentric ring patterns on older, lower leaves.
Yellow chlorotic halos around lesions; affected leaves senesce early.
Tubers may develop dark, sunken, circular lesions with raised borders.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers.
Ensure adequate nitrogen and potassium fertility; stressed plants are significantly more susceptible.
Rotate fields away from potatoes, tomatoes, and related nightshades for at least 3 years.
management: Avoid overhead irrigation late in the afternoon to minimize prolonged leaf wetness.
Harvest tubers only after vine desiccation and tuber skins have cured properly.
Consult local extension specialists for IPM-based fungicide timing.
Potato___Early_blight.limitations: Often confused with brown spot (Alternaria alternata) or physiological aging.

symptoms: Dark, water-soaked lesions expanding rapidly on foliage and stems.
White downy or cottony mildew visible on leaf undersides in high humidity.
Tubers exhibit irregular brown or purplish dry rot penetrating into tuber flesh.
prevention: Plant only certified seed potatoes with late blight inspection certificates.
Destroy potato cull piles, volunteer plants, and infected tubers prior to emergence.
Hill soil properly around tubers to create a physical barrier against washing spores.
management: Destroy heavily infested field hotspots to contain regional spore dispersal.
Ensure vines are completely dead before harvesting tubers to prevent tuber inoculation.
Report outbreaks to local agricultural extension agents immediately.
Potato___Late_blight.limitations: The historical pathogen of the Irish Potato Famine; causes devastatingly swift losses under wet, cool conditions.

symptoms: Sturdy stems with deep green compound leaves and intact leaflets.
Absence of necrotic patches, wilting, mosaic patterns, or leaf curling.
prevention: Maintain proper hilling, weed management, and balanced irrigation.
Scout fields periodically for Colorado potato beetles and aphid vectors.
management: Maintain standard agronomic fertilization and pest scouting protocols.
Potato___healthy.limitations: Foliage health does not guarantee absence of subterranean tuber defects or nematodes.

symptoms: Small, powdery, cinnamon-brown to reddish pustules scattered over both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, releasing powdery rust spores.
Leaves turn chlorotic and ragged as pustules coalesce in severe infections.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant or tolerant corn hybrids suitable for your geographical zone.
Maintain appropriate planting dates to avoid high summer spore flights.
management: Common rust rarely causes severe yield loss in commercial field corn; sweet corn is more vulnerable.
Fungicide intervention is usually only economically justified on high-value sweet corn or susceptible inbreds when conditions favor sustained epidemics.
Consult certified agronomists before chemical treatment.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.limitations: Can be confused with southern corn rust (Puccinia polysora), which has smaller, lighter orange pustules predominantly on upper leaf surfaces.
references: Iowa State University Extension - Corn Diseases

symptoms: Long, elliptical, grayish-green or tan cigar-shaped lesions (1 to 6 inches long) on leaves.
Lesions run parallel to leaf veins and may show dark fungal spores during damp weather.
Extensive leaf blighting reduces photosynthetic area, impairing grain fill.
prevention: Select resistant hybrids with documented multigenic or Ht-gene resistance.
Rotate crops with non-grasses (such as soybeans) to accelerate residue decomposition.
Incorporate or manage corn residue where conservation tillage allows.
management: Scout corn canopies around silking stage, especially under humid, moderate-temperature conditions (65-80°F).
Consult local university extension economic threshold guides before considering fungicide applications.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.limitations: Lesions may be atypical or restricted in resistant hybrid varieties.

symptoms: Long, arching, uniform green leaves with smooth venation and sharp margins.
No stripe lesions, rust pustules, or leaf tip scorch.
prevention: Ensure proper seedbed preparation, adequate soil nitrogen, and drainage.
Follow regional scouting timelines for early armyworm or stalk borer damage.
management: Continue standard fertilizer management and growth stage monitoring.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.limitations: Visual foliar assessment should be paired with soil and root evaluations.

symptoms: Dull, olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves, becoming puckered or distorted.
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely in mid-summer.
Rough, corky, olive-brown scabs or cracks on fruit surface.
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Freedom, Enterprise).
Rake, chop, or compost fallen autumn leaves to eliminate overwintering fungal pseudothecia.
Prune canopies annually to ensure sunlight and air reach all interior branches.
management: Apply protective or bio-fungicide sprays beginning at green tip through petal fall according to Mills scab infection periods.
Consult university pomology extension guidelines for spray timing.
Apple___Apple_scab.limitations: Foliar infection timing depends heavily on the duration of wetting hours and temperature (Mills chart).
references: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension

symptoms: Leaf spots known as 'frogeye': circular purple spots that enlarge with tan centers and purple margins.
Fruit rot starting as a brown spot that turns into concentric dark and light rings, eventually mummifying the apple.
Sunken, reddish-brown cankers on branches and tree limbs.
prevention: Prune out dead wood, fire blight strikes, and cankers at least 6 inches below visible infection.
Remove mummified apples hanging on the tree or lying on the orchard floor.
Sanitize pruning equipment between cuts.
management: Burn or deeply bury removed diseased wood and mummies to reduce inoculum reservoirs.
Consult local tree fruit specialists for recommended integrated spray programs.
Apple___Black_rot.limitations: Can be confused with cedar apple rust on leaves during very early lesion development.
references: Penn State Extension Tree Fruit Production Guide

symptoms: Clean, glossy, serrated green leaves with intact petioles and no fungal spotting.
Balanced shoot growth and healthy blossom/spur formation.
prevention: Conduct regular canopy pruning, clean weed rings, and balanced orchard nutrition.
Monitor for mite or aphid buildup on underside of leaves.
management: Maintain orchard sanitation and integrated orchard management schedules.
Apple___healthy.limitations: Does not rule out internal wood rots or subterranean root collar rot.

symptoms: Small, circular reddish-brown spots with dark borders on leaves.
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) visible inside leaf lesions in concentric arrangements.
Berries shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies covered in spore-producing bodies.
prevention: Prune vines in winter to open the trellis canopy for rapid leaf drying.
Remove and destroy mummified berries from the vine and vineyard floor during pruning.
Maintain effective weed control beneath vines to enhance low-level air movement.
management: Early season protective sprays from bud break through 4 to 6 weeks post-bloom are critical.
Consult viticulture extension specialists for disease-forecasting and spray schedules.
Grape___Black_rot.limitations: Severe berry infection leads to near total loss if not managed during the immediate post-bloom window.

symptoms: Broad, lobed green leaves with smooth venation and absence of necrotic spots or mildew.
Normal tendril and cane development.
prevention: Canopy management, shoot positioning, and timely leaf pulling in the fruiting zone.
management: Continue regular viticultural scouting and canopy maintenance.
Grape___healthy.limitations: Surface leaf appearance does not exclude latent viral infections like leafroll virus.

symptoms: Small, circular to irregular water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown to black.
Lower leaf surfaces often show slightly raised, blister-like centers.
Premature leaf drop exposing fruit to solar injury (sunscald).
Rough, circular raised scabs or warts on fruit.
prevention: Plant certified pathogen-free seed or resistant bell pepper cultivars.
Practice 2- to 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation and working among plants when wet.
management: Remove infected debris immediately after harvest.
Apply copper bactericides where permitted, keeping in mind potential bacterial copper resistance.
Consult local extension agents for resistance-breaking biorationals.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.limitations: Symptoms can resemble Cercospora leaf spot in initial stages.

symptoms: Vibrant green, smooth leaves with intact margins and firm petioles.
Good branching habit and vigorous flower bud set.
prevention: Provide even irrigation, avoid waterlogged soils, and maintain balanced fertility.
management: Routine scouting and standard crop management.
Pepper__bell___healthy.limitations: Visual foliar health should be supplemented with root and soil assessments.
references: UC Davis Vegetable Research & Information Center
